newsitem.title: GERMANY: German press accuse Paris of thwarting EMU.
newsitem.headline: German press accuse Paris of thwarting EMU.

text.p: German media cautioned on Tuesday that a call by France's new left-wing government to delay the stability pact intended to underpin European monetary union (EMU) seriously jeopardised plans for the euro.

The pact, proposed by German Finance Minister Theo Waigel to quell Germans' fears of swapping their beloved deutschemark for a possibly weaker single currency, is due for ratification at next week's European Union summit in Amsterdam.

But at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Luxembourg on Monday, French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said Paris needed time to study the pact -- which is designed to enforce fiscal restraint among EMU member states.

The daily Die Welt ran a front page story under the headline "Paris puts the euro stability pact on ice" and the Sueddeutsche Zeitung daily splashed the headline "Paris blocks stability pact for the euro" across its front page.
Commentators said France's proposal to think more about the pact was more than just a delaying tactic and that next week's summit was heading for crisis.
"France has plunged Europe into a dire situation," the Handelsblatt business daily said.
"If Paris seeks to put new elements into the stability pact that means nothing less than a delay (in EMU) as well as calling into question whether the stability pact will ever come about," it said.
Others scented a covert attempt to derail monetary union.

"It's not a question of protocol. The reality is that this is an attempt to mobilise monetary and financial policy to push back unemployment," the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung daily said in an editorial.

"The idea of a stability pact, which Germany and France had great trouble in developing, was to prevent exactly this kind of misuse of financial policy," it said, adding that France's leaders had returned to the "economic thinking of the 1960s".
The Bonn-based General Anzeiger daily also said "a real crisis" was in the offing at next week's EU summit.

"(French Prime Minister) Lionel Jospin has put the fight against unemployment at the heart of his campaign. If he wants to remain credible he must demand other EU partners follow suit," it commented. "Therein lies his dilemma."

"If Theo Waigel fails to rescue the stability pact he was primarily responsible for pushing through, citizens will lose any confidence they ever had in the stability of a future single currency," the General Anzeiger said.

However, the left-leaning Frankfurter Rundschau disagreed, saying France's demands for more time to think about the stability pact were justified and would not necessarily throw the 1999 launch date for EMU into doubt.

"This must be allowed and comes as no surprise as it is what the Socialists called for in their election campaign. The punctual launch of the euro would not yet be called into question by a delay in this agreement at Amsterdam," it said.
